title: Leaving GoDaddy: Step-by-Step Guide for Laravel and PHP Blogs
html:
Leaving GoDaddy takes under an hour if you know which files and database tables to grab before hitting cancel. When my GoDaddy Web Hosting Deluxe renewal jumped to ₹12,021.84, I packed up my 150-post Laravel blog, moved our media assets and database, and switched our DNS to Cloudflare without dropping a single URL. Here is the step-by-step developer guide to migrating away from GoDaddy cPanel without losing data, images, or SEO rankings.

Last updated: 10 Nov 2026. This guide is based on my hands-on migration of TrendsWheel from GoDaddy shared cPanel hosting. All steps reflect real cPanel interfaces, MySQL dumps, and DNS settings.

Before You Start: The 3 Rules of Leaving GoDaddy

Before touching any file or clicking cancel in your GoDaddy account, keep these three rules front and center:

  1. Do NOT cancel your hosting plan before backing up: GoDaddy's cancellation is permanent. Once you terminate the hosting account, your cPanel access, MySQL databases, and file manager are wiped immediately. Always take complete offsite backups first.
  2. Turn off Auto-Renew right away: GoDaddy often attempts automatic card charges up to 15 to 30 days before the actual expiration date. Go to Account Settings > Renewals & Billing, select your hosting plan, and turn Auto-Renew OFF so your card is not charged unexpectedly.
  3. Keep your domain DNS accessible: If your domain was purchased on GoDaddy alongside hosting, your DNS zone lives inside your GoDaddy domain management. You will point your nameservers to your new host (or Cloudflare), but keep your domain registered safely.

Step 1: Export Your MySQL Database (Without Timeouts)

In Laravel and PHP blogs, your entire article history, user accounts, categories, and tags live inside MySQL. On GoDaddy shared hosting, exporting large databases through phpMyAdmin often fails with a 504 Gateway Timeout.

Here is how to get a clean export safely:

  1. Log into your GoDaddy cPanel dashboard.
  2. Scroll to the Databases section and click phpMyAdmin.
  3. Select your blog database from the left sidebar.
  4. Click the Export tab at the top.
  5. Choose Custom - display all possible options (do not use Quick export for production databases).
  6. Under Tables, make sure all tables are selected (especially posts, categories, tags, and seo_redirects).
  7. Under Output, select Save output to a file and choose gzipped compression. Gzipping reduces a 50 MB database to around 5 MB, preventing browser timeouts during download.
  8. Click Export and save the .sql.gz file to your local machine.

Step 2: Download All Uploaded Images and Assets

Database text is useless without the accompanying images. In a standard Laravel setup, uploaded images live in storage/app/public/ (which is symlinked to public/storage/). In standard WordPress or custom PHP apps, they live under wp-content/uploads/ or public/uploads/.

  1. In cPanel, open File Manager.
  2. Navigate to your project root (e.g., /home/username/public_html/ or your Laravel directory).
  3. Locate the media folder: for Laravel, go to storage/app/public; for WordPress, go to wp-content/uploads.
  4. Select the folder and click Compress in the top toolbar. Choose Zip Archive.
  5. Once compressed, select the generated .zip file and click Download.
  6. Extract the zip locally. In TrendsWheel's case, this gave us 1,000 original post images ready for the new static setup.

Pro tip: Never download thousands of individual image files via FTP one by one. Shared hosting FTP throttles multiple file transfers. Zipping on the server and downloading one archive takes 30 seconds instead of an hour.

Step 3: Save Your Redirects and SEO Rules

One of the biggest mistakes developers make when leaving GoDaddy is forgetting their .htaccess redirect rules. If you had 301 redirects set up for older blog URLs, losing them will create 404 errors in Google Search Console and wipe out years of organic traffic.

  1. In cPanel File Manager, click Settings (top right corner).
  2. Check Show Hidden Files (dotfiles) and click Save.
  3. Open your public_html/.htaccess file and copy any custom RewriteRule or Redirect 301 lines.
  4. If you used a Laravel database redirects table (like seo_redirects), export those rows into a CSV or text file.
  5. When moving to static hosting like Cloudflare Pages, map these lines into a plain _redirects file in your public directory.

Step 4: Choose Your Next Destination

Before closing your GoDaddy account, decide where your site is moving:

Option Best For Monthly Cost Complexity
Cloudflare Pages (Static Export) Read-only blogs, content sites, Next.js / Astro ₹0 (Free) Moderate (requires code build)
Hostinger / Shared Host WordPress sites, traditional PHP apps ~₹149 - ₹299 / mo Low (one-click cPanel migration)
Hetzner / DigitalOcean VPS Complex Laravel apps with queues & active DB ~₹400 - ₹800 / mo High (requires Linux server management)

For TrendsWheel, moving to a static Next.js export on Cloudflare Pages was the obvious choice. Read my full breakdown in how I moved my Laravel blog to Cloudflare Pages (cost, speed, what broke).

Step 5: Switch Nameservers to Cloudflare

Once your new site or static export is ready to receive traffic, point your domain away from GoDaddy hosting:

  1. Create a free account on Cloudflare.
  2. Click Add a Site and enter your domain name (e.g., trendswheel.com).
  3. Select the Free plan. Cloudflare will automatically scan and import your existing DNS records.
  4. Cloudflare will provide two nameservers (e.g., ns1.cloudflare.com, ns2.cloudflare.com).
  5. Go to GoDaddy Domain Portfolio > Manage DNS > Nameservers.
  6. Click Change Nameservers, choose I'll use my own nameservers, and paste the two Cloudflare nameserver addresses.
  7. Save the changes. DNS propagation usually takes between 15 minutes and 2 hours.

Step 6: Cancel GoDaddy Hosting and Confirm

Only after your new site is live, DNS has fully propagated, and you have confirmed that your images and articles load smoothly:

  1. Log into your GoDaddy account.
  2. Go to Renewals & Billing.
  3. Find your Web Hosting plan.
  4. Click Cancel Renewal or Delete Product.
  5. Confirm the cancellation. You have successfully freed your site from recurring renewal charges.

The Real Cost Comparison

Here is what leaving GoDaddy saves over 3 years:

Timeframe Staying on GoDaddy Deluxe Moving to Cloudflare Pages Total Saved
Year 1 Renewal ₹12,021.84 ₹0 ₹12,021.84
Year 2 Renewal ~₹12,800.00 ₹0 ₹24,821.84
Year 3 Renewal ~₹13,500.00 ₹0 ₹38,321.84

Who Should (and Shouldn't) Follow This Guide

  • Follow this guide if: You are on a cPanel plan facing steep renewal hikes, your site is primarily content-driven, and you want to reclaim control over your data and hosting costs.
  • Do NOT follow this guide blindly if: You host active client email accounts on GoDaddy cPanel webmail without exporting them first. Always migrate your custom domain email (to Google Workspace, Zoho, or MXroute) before terminating the hosting account.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will leaving GoDaddy hurt my Google search rankings?

Not if you preserve your exact URLs, slugs, and 301 redirects. In our migration, every single post URL and image path remained identical, preventing broken link penalties.

Can I leave GoDaddy hosting but keep my domain registered there?

Yes. Web hosting and domain registration are separate products. You can cancel your GoDaddy web hosting while keeping your domain name registered with GoDaddy, simply changing the DNS nameservers.

How long does the whole migration take?

Exporting your database and downloading media takes about 15 minutes. Setting up your new host or static build takes 1 to 2 hours. DNS propagation takes another 1 to 2 hours.
